extracted.intended_audience: Presbytery members, theologians, and readers interested in reformation-era ecclesiastical/political controversies
extracted.subtask_description: A presbyterial polemic/testimony arguing against the 'Seceders' doctrine concerning allegiance, magistracy, and the relation between providential and preceptive will of God. It evaluates when civil rulers are lawfully to be acknowledged and what qualifications and scriptural bases are required for lawful magistracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between providential and preceptive will of God
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a real and necessary distinction between God's providential will (who providence places in power) and his preceptive will (who God authorizes and commands to be magistrate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues this distinction is 'irreversibly fixed' and crucial: providential elevation of a ruler does not automatically make that ruler lawful in the preceptive sense. Scriptural citations (Ezek., Hos., Deut., etc.) and historical examples (David, Absalom, Solomon, Joash, Jeroboam, Elisha) are adduced to show that possession of power by providence or popular consent does not equate to divine authorization by precept. Failure to respect this distinction leads to making all providential magistrates 'preceptive' and is judged a grave error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawfulness of swearing allegiance when government is acknowledged by the people
rubrics_metrics.description: If a government is acknowledged by the people and has the essentials of a lawful constitution, it is lawful to swear allegiance to it; refusal to swear must be justified consistently with one's principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contends Seceders contradict themselves by acknowledging the present government as lawful yet refusing to swear allegiance. The oaths of allegiance bind to 'own the lawfulness of the government' and to maintain it according to its constitution; where an oath conflicts with covenant obligations, it is the constitution (sanctified by popular acknowledgment) that causes inconsistency, not the abstract oath. Thus reconciliation is possible and refusal is inconsistent unless one can show the government is unlawful in constitution or practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of scriptural and covenantal qualifications for lawful magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a lawful Christian magistrate one must possess scriptural and covenant qualifications in addition to the consent of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery points to coronation oaths and parliamentary acts (James VI, Charles I, Acts cited) requiring monarchs to swear to maintain the true religion, to consent to the National Covenant and Solemn League, to preserve Presbyterian government and approved confessional standards, and that office-bearers be 'men of known affection unto, and of approved fidelity and integrity.' Thus legitimacy is not purely providential/popular but requires conformity to reformation/covenanted standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of rulers whose constitution or administration contradicts God's law
rubrics_metrics.description: When a ruler's constitution or habitual administration conflicts with God's revealed will, it is lawful and sometimes commendable to refuse acknowledgment and obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text marshals Old Testament examples (Saul, Jeroboam, Baasha, Libnah, the people who rejected Absalom) where persons or groups disowned rulers for apostasy or wickedness. The author argues that scripture both condemns setting up rulers contrary to God's precept and justifies disowning such rulers; therefore acknowledgement of such rulers by others cannot be deemed simply lawful obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper exegesis: scriptural texts only establish obedience to lawful commands, not obedience to sinful authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Texts cited by Seceders prove duty to obey lawful rulers in lawful commands, but do not establish a duty to obey, for conscience' sake, rulers whose constitution or practice is sinful and contrary to revealed law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Presbytery accuses the Associate Presbytery of misapplying scripture: the quoted passages show the duty to obey lawful authority but do not support submission to authorities that are sinful in constitution or course. Hence theological interpretation must distinguish obedience to lawful commands from endorsement of sinful constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath-content and possible limiting phrases to reconcile conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: If oaths of allegiance are framed or limited (for example, 'so long as the body politic is pleased to acknowledge the supreme magistrate'), some scruples of conscience might be eased—but such limitations reveal the Seceders' deeper inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes Seceders' stated difficulty is fear that an oath would bind them to future, possibly popish, rulers. He observes that inserting temporal or conditional limitations into oaths could make them more acceptable to Seceders, but treats this more as demonstrating their underlying anarchical principle than as a true solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of civil and ecclesiastical authority in the English crown (no artificial civil/ecclesiastical split)
rubrics_metrics.description: The English king's office is presented as inherently both civil and ecclesiastical; attempts to separate these (civil vs ecclesiastical authority) are deemed chimerical and self-contradictory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes Seceders for inventing a distinction between the king's civil and ecclesiastical authority in order to avoid acknowledging the established constitution. He argues that the king, as head, is 'head and chief prelate' with power both civil and ecclesiastical; to acknowledge one aspect while denying the other is a logical absurdity and a deception of conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with reformation covenants and the Solemn League and Covenant
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles about magistracy must be consistent with the national and reformation covenants: duties include preserving reformed religion, extirpating popery and prelacy, preserving parliament rights and kingdom liberties, and maintaining the covenanted union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text compares Seceders' principles unfavorably with articles of the Solemn League and Covenant, arguing they are inconsistent with each article (preservation of reformed religion, extirpation of popery/prelacy, defense of parliamentary rights, union of kingdoms, etc.). The author contends that claiming to hold reformation principles while accepting providential/popular authority irrespective of its religion is a contradiction and betrayal of covenant obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scriptural and historical examples as decisive tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Scriptural narratives and historical practice are valid tests to determine whether possession of power equals lawful title; many examples show actual possession by providence/popular consent did not equal lawful preceptive right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists multiple biblical instances (David's reign, Absalom's revolt, Solomon/Adonijah, Joash/Athalid, the Babylonish captivity, Saul's rejection, Elisha's disowning of a king) and examples of national practice to show that lawful title and moral right may persist despite loss of actual possession. These instances are used as hermeneutic rules to refute the Seceders' identification of providential possession with legitimate preceptive authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political consequence criterion: principles must not open the door to Jacobitism or apostasy
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle that obliges universal acknowledgement of any prevailing government — even popish or prelatic — is judged dangerous because it exposes the nation to apostasy and Jacobitism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that if everyone is bound to acknowledge whichever government prevails, then a putative popish pretender set up by a faction would be lawfully to be acknowledged by all, undermining reformation safeguards. Thus an evaluative criterion for political doctrine is whether it preserves the religious and constitutional protections of the covenanted reformation rather than facilitating its overthrow.
